newsitem.title: USA: PairGain falls on price, technology fears.
newsitem.headline: PairGain falls on price, technology fears.

text.p: Shares of PairGain Technologies Inc, a leading supplier of high-speed corporate data access equipment, retreated well below its 52-week low Monday as analysts cited mounting concerns on multiple fronts.
PairGain stock fell to 15-3/4, down 1-1/2, Monday and was the most actively traded Nasdaq issue for the second day running, with volume nearing 16 million shares.
Analysts cited downward pricing pressures in its core business but also growing fears that PairGain has failed to keep pace with new technology developments in its market.
Several Wall Street analysts cut their near-term earnings outlook Monday but kept the stock's rating at buy or outperform. Some argued the recent selloff has been overdone.

UBS Securities analyst Nikos Teodosopoulous kept his buy rating, but citing the tightening pricing environment, cut his PairGain earnings estimates to $0.73 per share from $0.81 for 1997 and to $0.93 from $1.05 for 1998, his office said.

PairGain is known for its roughly 70 percent market share in a technology known as High bit-rate Digital Subscriber Line, or HDSL, which has become popular among corporate users as a low-cost replacement for high-speed T-1 phone lines.
PairGain officials acknowledged at a recent Hambrecht & Quist investor conference that they were seeing rising HDSL price pressures, according to Lehman analyst Tim Luke.
These concerns were stoked anew last Thursday when another HDSL supplier, Teltrend Inc, warned of flat revenue growth for its fourth fiscal quarter ending in July, he said.
Adding fuel to the sell-off are warnings from industry analysts that the HDSL market is seeing signs of aging.
The action is seen as shifting to an emerging data transmission method called Asymetrical Digital Subscriber Line (ADSL), with data rates up to 10 times faster than HDSL.
PairGain has yet to reveal a complete ADSL strategy, analysts said.
The company did not return calls seeking comment.

"They are going through a change-over in technology," telecom industry analyst Daniel Briere of TeleChoice Inc said. "PairGain has built a very solid business selling HDSL, a mature technology that is low-cost and popular with telcos."
"That's why people have loved them," Briere said. "But right now the marketplace sees other competitors as having the jump on PairGain in the emerging ADSL market," he said.
Putting further pressure on PairGain stock was news Monday of contract wins by several companies seen as direct or potential competitors to PairGain.

Orckit Communications Ltd, a rival HDSL supplier that has been nibbling at PairGain's overseas market share, said it won a deal to supply China's Postal and Telecom agency, giving Orckit a foothold in the emerging Asian market.
"Orckit's approach has been to go after the European and foreign markets because that's where they felt PairGain's market share is weakest," Briere said of Israeli-based Orckit.

In addition, Bell Atlantic Corp said Monday it plans an ADSL service in its local calling region by mid-1998 using equipment from Westell Technologies Inc and DSC Communications Corp, a carrier equipment supplier.
To date, analysts said PairGain has deferred putting forth a complete ADSL strategy by saying that the company is prepared to offer ADSL products as the market develops.

PairGain has preferred to develop its ADSL technology in-house and so far has declined to beef up its ADSL offerings by going outside the company to make acquisitions of firms like NetSpeed or Peformance Telecom, Briere said.
"I am not sure if its response is strong enough for the marketplace when contracts are being awarded today," he said.
ADSL is targeted at residential consumers, not corporate users, and remains significantly more expensive than HDSL.
But ADSL's exponentially higher speed and the prospect of widescale regional deployment by phone carriers has put pressure on PairGain to develop its own ADSL alternative.

The dozens of ADSL product announcements made at Networld+Interop, a major network equipment industry trade show held in Las Vegas two weeks ago, have added to a sense of rising momentum for the potential HDSL replacement technology.
